goals: State the standard definition of a nation and name its elements
Distinguish a nation from a race, a language group and a religion
Explain the description of a nation as an imagined community
Describe the role of nationalism in history, including its link with conflict
Explain national self-determination and the problems of applying it

slides.narration: What makes a group of people a nation? In this part we define a nation and its elements, see why it is called an imagined community, look at the role of nationalism in history, and ask why giving every group its own state is hard.

slides.heading: What a nation is

rows: A large group of people who see themselves as a community with a shared identity, and who wish to govern themselves
Beliefs, a history, a homeland or territory and political ideals
Not simply a race, a language group or a religion
The people of Veldan, who speak three languages and follow four faiths, still see themselves as one nation

slides.narration: A nation is a large group of people who see themselves as a community with a shared identity, and who wish to govern themselves. They share beliefs, a history, a homeland or territory, and political ideals. In imagined Veldan, people speak three languages and follow four faiths, yet most see themselves as one nation.

slides.narration: Recall the standard definition of a nation.

slides.heading: A nation is not a race, a language group or a religion

rows: A group classed together by supposed common ancestry
Nations include people of many backgrounds
People who speak the same language
A nation may have several languages
A nation may include many faiths
A community with a shared identity and a wish to govern itself
Rests on belief, history, territory and ideals

slides.narration: A nation is not the same as a race, a language group or a religion. A race is classed by supposed common ancestry, a language group shares a language, and a religion shares a faith. A nation may include people of many backgrounds, languages and faiths, and rests on belief, history, territory and ideals.

slides.narration: A nation is sometimes called an imagined community, a phrase associated with Benedict Anderson. Members never meet most of the other members, yet they feel that they belong together. This does not mean the nation is unreal. It is imagined because it rests on a shared feeling and not on personal contact.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: is it a nation?
slides.body_md: Test four imagined groups against the standard definition.

Does it have a **homeland** and a **political aim**?

A large community with shared identity that wishes to govern itself
The scattered Corlen traders, with no common homeland
They share language and customs but lack a territory they all call home
Not a large community with a homeland or a political aim
The Hallow people, who see themselves as distinct and ask for self-rule

slides.narration: Let us test four imagined groups. The people of Veldan fit the idea of a nation. The scattered Corlen traders share language and customs but have no common homeland, so they fit only partly. A school chess club is not a nation. The Hallow people see themselves as distinct, and their claim raises the question of self-determination.

slides.narration: Nationalism has shaped history in several ways. In nineteenth century Europe it helped to unify states, and Germany and Italy were unified about eighteen seventy and eighteen seventy one. After the First World War it contributed to the break up of the Austro Hungarian and Ottoman empires. In Asia and Africa it powered anti colonial movements, including India's freedom struggle.

slides.narration: Nationalism has bound people together and helped them win freedom. It has also been linked with wars and with the exclusion of some groups. Both are true, because the same feeling of belonging can include some people and shut out others. A student should give examples of both effects and avoid a one sided claim.

slides.narration: National self determination is the claim of a nation to govern itself and to have its own state. It became important after the First World War, when many people held the idea of one culture, one state. In an imagined case, the Hallow people of Ostira ask for a state in which they make the laws.

sections.body_md:
A **nation** is a large group of people who see themselves as a **community** with a shared identity, and who wish to **govern themselves**. The elements commonly named are shared **beliefs**, **history**, **territory**, shared **political ideals** and a **common political identity**.

A nation is **not the same** as a race, a language group or a religion; many nations include people of different languages and faiths.

sections.body_md: A nation is sometimes described as an **imagined community**, a phrase associated with **Benedict Anderson**. Members never meet most of the other members, yet they feel that they **belong together**. sections.heading: 3. Nationalism in history
sections.body_md: Nationalism helped to **unify** states in nineteenth-century Europe; **Germany** and **Italy** were unified about **1870 and 1871**. After the **First World War** (1914 to 1918) it contributed to the break-up of the **Austro-Hungarian** and **Ottoman** empires. It powered **anti-colonial movements** in Asia and Africa, including India's freedom struggle. It has also been linked with **conflict** and wars.

key_terms.definition_md: A strong sense of belonging to a nation and loyalty to its identity and aims.
A movement in which a people under foreign rule demands freedom and self-government.

sections.heading: 4. National self-determination
sections.body_md:
**National self-determination** is the claim of a nation to **govern itself** and have its **own state**. It became important after the First World War, when the idea of **one culture, one state** gained force.

The difficulty is that almost every state has **minorities**. Giving each group its own state would create new minorities, and **ever smaller states** are neither practical nor peaceful. Democratic states can instead protect minority identities by rights.

key_terms.definition_md: The claim of a nation to govern itself and to have its own state.
A group within a state that differs from the majority in language, religion or culture.

sections.heading: 5. Accommodating diversity
sections.body_md:
A democratic state can accommodate diversity by **recognising and protecting** the identities of minorities, through **constitutional rights** for linguistic, religious and cultural groups, and **group rights** alongside individual rights.

In India, states were reorganised mainly on **linguistic lines in 1956**. **Article 29** lets a section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture conserve it. **Article 30** lets religious and linguistic minorities establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

sections.heading: 6. Pluralism, unity and Tagore
sections.body_md:
**Pluralism** is the idea that a nation can include many cultures and identities, and that **unity need not mean uniformity**.

Some argue that strong national unity needs a **shared culture**. Others argue that unity is best built by **respecting diversity**. A student presents both with reasons and then judges.

**Rabindranath Tagore** valued the freedom struggle but held that **patriotism should not override humanity**; a narrow nationalism may shut out others and overlook minorities.

The condition of everyone being the same in language, culture or custom.
A nationalism that places the nation above all else, including concern for humanity.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying a nation is a race or a religion: nations include people of different languages and faiths.
- Calling an imagined community unreal: it is real in its effects but rests on shared feeling.
- Calling nationalism only good or only bad: state both its unifying and its divisive effects.
- Saying every group should get a state: explain minorities and the limits of ever smaller states.
- Treating unity and uniformity as the same.
- Mixing up Articles 29 and 30.
- Quoting Tagore: state his view in your own words.

**Tips:** begin with the standard definition; give a short imagined example; present both views, then judge with reasons.

cards.front_md: What is a **nation**?
cards.back_md: A large group of people who see themselves as a community with a shared identity, and who wish to govern themselves.

cards.front_md: Name the elements commonly used to describe a nation
cards.back_md: Shared beliefs, history, territory, shared political ideals and a common political identity.

cards.front_md: Is a nation the same as a race?
cards.back_md: No. Many nations include people of different backgrounds.

cards.front_md: Is a nation the same as a language group?
cards.back_md: No. A nation may have several languages.

cards.front_md: Is a nation the same as a religion?
cards.back_md: No. A nation may include many faiths.

cards.front_md: What is an **imagined community**?
cards.back_md: A description of a nation as a community whose members never meet most of the others, yet feel they belong together.

cards.front_md: With whom is the phrase **imagined community** associated?
cards.back_md: Benedict Anderson.

cards.front_md: Does imagined mean unreal?
cards.back_md: No. The community is real in its effects; it rests on shared feeling and not on personal contact.

cards.front_md: What is **territory** as an element of a nation?
cards.back_md: The land that members regard as their homeland.

cards.front_md: What is a **common political identity**?
cards.back_md: The shared sense of belonging together as citizens of one political community.

cards.front_md: What is **nationalism**?
cards.back_md: A strong sense of belonging to a nation and loyalty to its identity and aims.

cards.front_md: Which two states were unified in Europe about 1870 and 1871?
cards.back_md: Germany and Italy.

cards.front_md: Which empires broke up after the First World War?
cards.back_md: The Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires.

cards.front_md: When was the First World War fought?
cards.back_md: From 1914 to 1918.

cards.front_md: What role did nationalism play in Asia and Africa?
cards.back_md: It powered anti-colonial movements, including India's freedom struggle.

cards.front_md: What is an **anti-colonial movement**?
cards.back_md: A movement in which a people under foreign rule demands freedom and self-government.

cards.front_md: Is nationalism only a force for good or only for harm?
cards.back_md: Neither. It has unified and freed people and has also been linked with conflict and wars.

cards.front_md: What is **national self-determination**?
cards.back_md: The claim of a nation to govern itself and to have its own state.

cards.front_md: What idea gained force after the First World War?
cards.back_md: One culture, one state: each national group should have its own state.

cards.front_md: What is a **minority**?
cards.back_md: A group within a state that differs from the majority in language, religion or culture.

cards.front_md: Why is a state for every group hard to achieve?
cards.back_md: Almost every state has minorities, and ever smaller states are neither practical nor peaceful.

cards.front_md: How can a democratic state accommodate diversity?
cards.back_md: By recognising and protecting the identities of minorities, through constitutional rights and group rights beside individual rights.

cards.front_md: What are **group rights**?
cards.back_md: Rights that protect the language, religion or culture of a community as a community, alongside individual rights.

cards.front_md: What are **individual rights**?
cards.back_md: Rights held by each person, protecting equal treatment.

cards.front_md: What happened to states in India in 1956?
cards.back_md: They were reorganised mainly along linguistic lines.

cards.front_md: What does **Article 29** provide, in brief?
cards.back_md: Any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture may conserve it.

cards.front_md: What does **Article 30** provide, in brief?
cards.back_md: Religious and linguistic minorities may establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

cards.front_md: What is **pluralism**?
cards.back_md: The idea that a nation can include many cultures and identities, and that unity need not mean uniformity.

cards.front_md: What is the difference between unity and uniformity?
cards.back_md: Unity is a bond among people; uniformity is being the same. Unity need not mean uniformity.

cards.front_md: What view says unity needs a shared culture?
cards.back_md: The view that common language and customs give people a shared bond.

cards.front_md: What view says unity is built by respecting diversity?
cards.back_md: The view that people are loyal when every community has a fair place.

cards.front_md: What was Rabindranath Tagore's criticism of narrow nationalism?
cards.back_md: He valued the freedom struggle but held that patriotism should not override humanity.

questions.stem_md: In political theory, a nation is best described as

options.text_md: any group of people who happen to live inside the same borders
a large group of people who see themselves as one community with a shared identity and who wish to govern themselves
a group of people who all belong to a single race
the government and the officials of a country

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a large group of people who see themselves as one community with a shared identity and who wish to govern themselves. A nation is a large group who regard themselves as a community with a shared identity and a wish to govern themselves. Living inside borders does not make people a nation, race is not the test, and a government is only one institution of a state.

questions.stem_md: The people of the imagined country of Veldan speak three languages and follow four faiths, yet most of them feel that they belong to one Veldanese nation with a common homeland. What does this show?

options.text_md: Veldan cannot be a nation because it has several languages
A nation must always share one faith
Nations are formed only by people of one race
A nation need not be a single language group or a single religious community

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A nation need not be a single language group or a single religious community. Veldan shows that a nation can contain several languages and faiths, so it is not the same as a language group, a religion or a race. The other statements wrongly treat language, faith or race as a necessary condition.

questions.stem_md: The description of a nation as an imagined community is associated with

options.text_md: Benedict Anderson
T. H. Marshall
Isaiah Berlin
John Rawls

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Benedict Anderson. The phrase imagined community is associated with Benedict Anderson. Marshall is linked with the theory of citizenship rights, Berlin with the idea of two kinds of liberty and Rawls with the theory of justice.

questions.stem_md: Why is a nation sometimes called an imagined community?

options.text_md: Because nations exist only in stories and have no real effect
Because the members of a nation all know each other personally
Because members never meet most of the other members, yet they feel that they belong together
Because nations are invented by their governments overnight

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Because members never meet most of the other members, yet they feel that they belong together. The phrase points out that in a large nation people cannot know most of their fellow members, but they still feel part of one community. It does not mean that nations are unreal, nor that members know one another, nor that governments invent them overnight.

questions.stem_md: Which list gives elements through which a nation is commonly described?

options.text_md: Shared surname, shared occupation and shared income
A single race, a single language and a single religion in every case
Shared beliefs, history, territory, shared political ideals and a common political identity
An army, a currency and a flag only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Shared beliefs, history, territory, shared political ideals and a common political identity. Shared beliefs, history, territory, political ideals and a common political identity are the usual elements. A shared surname or income is not one, and a single race, language or religion is not required in every nation. An army or a flag may be symbols of a state but do not by themselves make a nation.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Corlen traders live scattered across five different countries. They share a language and many customs, but they have no land that they all regard as a common homeland. Which element of a nation do they lack most clearly?

options.text_md: A shared territory or homeland
A shared language
A shared set of customs
A shared occupation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A shared territory or homeland. The traders have a language and customs in common, but no territory that they regard as a homeland, which is one of the usual elements of a nation. The other options are things they do have.

questions.stem_md: In the nineteenth century, nationalism helped to bring together several smaller states into new unified states in

options.text_md: Britain and Spain, completed about 1500
Egypt and Persia, completed about 1900
Brazil and Chile, completed about 1920
Germany and Italy, completed about 1870 and 1871

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Germany and Italy, completed about 1870 and 1871. The unification of Germany and Italy, completed about 1870 and 1871, is the standard example from nineteenth-century Europe. The other pairs and dates are not examples of unification through nationalism in this period.

questions.stem_md: Which large empires broke up after the First World War, in a period when nationalism was a strong force?

options.text_md: The Roman and Mongol empires
The Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires
The Mughal and Maurya empires
The British and French empires, completely, by 1919

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires. The Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires broke up after the war of 1914 to 1918. The Roman, Mongol, Mughal and Maurya empires belong to much earlier times, and the British and French empires did not end in 1919.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined colony of Kelvar, ruled for a century by a distant foreign power, people of many faiths begin a movement saying that they are one nation and must govern themselves. Which historical development does this movement resemble?

options.text_md: An anti-colonial movement of the kind found in Asia and Africa, such as India's freedom struggle
The unification of states in nineteenth-century Europe
The break-up of the Austro-Hungarian empire
A movement to extend the rule of a colonial power

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** An anti-colonial movement of the kind found in Asia and Africa, such as India's freedom struggle. A people under foreign rule who demand self-government as a nation resemble the anti-colonial movements of Asia and Africa, including India's freedom struggle. Unification joined existing states, the Austro-Hungarian break-up was the end of an empire in Europe, and the movement does not seek to extend foreign rule.

questions.stem_md: Two students in the imagined Greenfield school debate nationalism. Tessa says it has only ever brought freedom. Imre says it has only ever brought war. Which comment is the most accurate?

options.text_md: Tessa is correct, because nationalism has never been linked with conflict
Nationalism has helped to unify states and to win freedom, and it has also been linked with conflict and wars
Imre is correct, because nationalism has never helped any people
Nationalism has had no effect on history

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Nationalism has helped to unify states and to win freedom, and it has also been linked with conflict and wars. History shows both sides: nationalism helped to unify states and to power freedom struggles, and it has also been linked with conflicts and wars. A claim that it has only one effect ignores the other, and it has certainly affected history.

questions.stem_md: National self-determination is the claim of a nation to

options.text_md: conquer its neighbours
be governed by a foreign power
govern itself and have its own state
abolish all borders

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** govern itself and have its own state. National self-determination is the claim of a nation to govern itself and to have its own state. It is not a claim to conquest, to rule by a foreign power or to abolish borders.

questions.stem_md: After the First World War the idea of national self-determination became important mainly because it

options.text_md: was meant to remove all minorities from every state
ended the need for any state
was written into the laws of every country at once
was used to argue that each national group should have its own state, an idea sometimes put as one culture, one state

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** was used to argue that each national group should have its own state, an idea sometimes put as one culture, one state. After the war, people argued that each national group should have its own state, an idea often summed up as one culture, one state. It did not remove minorities or the need for states, and it was not adopted at once as law by every country.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined country of Ostira, the Hallow people, who regard themselves as a distinct nation, ask for a state of their own in which they alone make the laws. Their demand is an example of

options.text_md: a claim to naturalisation
a claim to universal adult franchise
a claim to judicial review
a claim to national self-determination

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a claim to national self-determination. A national group that asks to govern itself and to have its own state is making a claim to national self-determination. Naturalisation concerns foreigners, franchise is the right to vote and judicial review is the power of courts to examine laws.

questions.stem_md: Why is it not practical to give every national group its own state?

options.text_md: Because no group is ever large enough to form a state
Because every state already has just one kind of people
Almost every state contains minorities, so new states would still contain minorities, and ever smaller states are neither practical nor peaceful
Because states cannot change their borders by any means

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Almost every state contains minorities, so new states would still contain minorities, and ever smaller states are neither practical nor peaceful. Peoples are mixed, so almost every state has minorities, and new states would soon have minorities of their own. Ever smaller states are not practical or peaceful. It is not true that all states have one kind of people or that no border can ever change.

questions.stem_md: The imagined country of Dornel is divided into two new states to satisfy two groups. Each new state still has a sizeable group of people who belong to the other community. What does this show about the aim of one culture, one state?

options.text_md: It is easy to achieve, because the groups can always be separated completely
Dividing states again and again may still leave minorities in every new state, so it cannot settle the matter
Minorities disappear once a state is divided
A new state never contains more than one group

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Dividing states again and again may still leave minorities in every new state, so it cannot settle the matter. The new states each still contain a minority, which shows that division does not remove diversity and could be repeated without end. Groups cannot always be separated completely, minorities do not vanish, and new states may contain several groups.

questions.stem_md: A pamphlet in the imagined country of Dornel says that only people of one ancestry may call themselves Dornelian. Which idea does this contradict?

options.text_md: A nation is not the same as a race, and many nations include people of different backgrounds
A nation has a homeland
A nation has a shared history
A nation may wish to govern itself

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A nation is not the same as a race, and many nations include people of different backgrounds. The pamphlet treats nation and ancestry as one, but a nation is not the same as a race and may include people of many backgrounds. The other statements are accepted features of a nation, so the pamphlet does not contradict them.

questions.stem_md: Citizens of the imagined country of Marenth belong to many faiths and speak several languages, but they hold common political ideals such as equal rights and a government chosen by all. Which element of a nation does this describe?

options.text_md: A shared race
Shared political ideals, which help to give a common political identity
A shared religion
A shared surname

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Shared political ideals, which help to give a common political identity. Common ideals such as equal rights and an elected government are the shared political ideals that give people a common political identity. They are shown to hold even where faith and language differ, so race, religion and surnames are not the source of the unity here.

questions.stem_md: Villagers in the imagined country of Ostira who live far from one another all celebrate the same harvest festival and tell the same stories about a founding hero. Which statement about their unity is most accurate?

options.text_md: Festivals cannot create any feeling of community
Only the army can unite people who live far apart
Stories about the past have no connection with nations
Shared belief and a shared history help them to feel part of one community even though they never meet

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Shared belief and a shared history help them to feel part of one community even though they never meet. Shared beliefs and a shared history are elements that help members of a large community to feel that they belong together without meeting, which is the point of calling it imagined. Festivals and stories do help, so the denials are wrong, and an army is not the only means of unity.

questions.stem_md: One way in which a democratic state can accommodate diversity is by

options.text_md: recognising and protecting the identities of minorities, for example through constitutional rights
requiring every citizen to give up his or her language
refusing to recognise any group
removing all minority institutions

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** recognising and protecting the identities of minorities, for example through constitutional rights. A democratic state can accommodate diversity by recognising and protecting minority identities, such as through constitutional rights. Forcing people to give up a language, refusing recognition or removing institutions do the opposite.

questions.stem_md: A law of the imagined country of Marenth lets the small Daravi community hold its own festivals and teach its own songs in its schools, while every Marenthi also has equal rights before the law. The first part of the law is best called

options.text_md: an individual right to vote
a duty to pay taxes
a group right, protecting the culture of a community
a right of governments to control culture

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a group right, protecting the culture of a community. Protecting the festivals and songs of a community as a community is a group right, and it sits beside the individual right of equal treatment. Voting is a different individual right, paying taxes is a duty and the law does not give governments control over culture.

questions.stem_md: In India, the reorganisation of states mainly along linguistic lines was carried out in
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 1956. The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 reorganised states mainly on linguistic lines. The other years do not mark this reorganisation.

questions.stem_md: Article 29 of the Constitution of India protects

options.text_md: the right of any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture to conserve it
the right to move freely throughout the country
the right to vote at eighteen
the power of the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the right of any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture to conserve it. Article 29 protects the interests of minorities by allowing a section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture to conserve it. Free movement, the voting age and the President's powers are provided elsewhere.

questions.stem_md: Article 30 of the Constitution of India gives religious and linguistic minorities the right to

options.text_md: form a separate army
issue their own currency
make laws for the whole country
establish and administer educational institutions of their choice

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. Article 30 gives minorities, whether religious or linguistic, the right to set up and run educational institutions of their choice. It does not give any group an army, a currency or the power to legislate for the country.

questions.stem_md: Parents belonging to a linguistic minority in an imagined town in India open a primary school that teaches in their own language. Which constitutional provision does this activity most closely relate to?

options.text_md: Article 19, on freedom of speech
Article 30, on educational institutions of minorities
Article 14, on equality before the law
Article 368, on amendment of the Constitution

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Article 30, on educational institutions of minorities. Setting up a school that conserves a minority language relates to Article 30, which gives minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions, and to Article 29 on conserving language and culture. The other Articles deal with different matters.

questions.stem_md: Pluralism is the idea that

options.text_md: a nation can include many cultures and identities, and unity need not mean uniformity
every citizen must follow one culture
only the majority has a culture
a nation can have no identity at all

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a nation can include many cultures and identities, and unity need not mean uniformity. Pluralism holds that many cultures and identities can exist within one nation and that unity does not require sameness. It is the opposite of insisting on one culture, and it does not deny that a nation can have an identity.

questions.stem_md: What is the difference between unity and uniformity?

options.text_md: They are the same thing
Unity is people feeling bound together, while uniformity is everyone being the same in culture or language
Unity needs one language, while uniformity needs several
Unity means no laws, while uniformity means many laws

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Unity is people feeling bound together, while uniformity is everyone being the same in culture or language. Unity is a bond among people, which can exist even when they differ, while uniformity means that everyone is made the same. They are not the same, and neither is defined by the number of languages or laws.

questions.stem_md: The government of the imagined country of Veldan orders that every school must teach in the Veldanic language only and that minority festivals must not be held in public. Which view of nationhood does this order reflect, and what criticism might be made?

options.text_md: A pluralist view; critics say it gives minorities too much
A view that nations do not exist; critics say it is too weak
A view that unity requires one culture; critics say it ignores the identities and rights of minorities
A view that all states should be abolished; critics say it is too short

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A view that unity requires one culture; critics say it ignores the identities and rights of minorities. An order that allows one language and one set of customs reflects the view that unity needs uniformity, and critics argue it ignores the identities and rights of minorities. It is not pluralist, since it denies difference, and it does not claim that nations or states do not exist.

questions.stem_md: The imagined constitution of Kessar says that every community may run its own schools and festivals, and that every individual also has equal rights before the law. This combines

options.text_md: group rights with the abolition of individual rights
individual rights without any group recognition
neither group rights nor individual rights
group rights alongside individual rights

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** group rights alongside individual rights. Allowing communities to keep their schools and festivals protects group rights, and equal rights before the law protects individuals, so the two are combined. The other options describe constitutions that drop one side or both.

questions.stem_md: Rabindranath Tagore's criticism of narrow nationalism held that

options.text_md: nationalism is the highest value, above everything else
the freedom struggle was a mistake
nations should have no culture
patriotism should not be placed above humanity

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** patriotism should not be placed above humanity. Tagore valued the freedom struggle but held that love of one's country should not override concern for humanity. He did not rank the nation above all else, he did not call the freedom struggle a mistake and he did not say that nations should have no culture.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined Greenfield school debate, Rohan says that love of the country means welcoming only people who think like him and ignoring the suffering of others abroad. Which reply fits Tagore's criticism of narrow nationalism?

Rohan should abandon his country altogether
Love of one's country is compatible with concern for humanity, and should not make us blind to the suffering of others
Tagore believed that debate is wrong

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Love of one's country is compatible with concern for humanity, and should not make us blind to the suffering of others. Tagore's criticism was that narrow nationalism puts the nation above humanity, so the fitting reply is that patriotism should go along with concern for others. Saying nothing outside the country matters repeats the narrow view, and Tagore did not ask people to abandon their country or oppose debate.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined meeting in Ostira, one speaker says that strong national unity needs a shared culture. Another says that unity is best built by respecting diversity. Which response is the most balanced?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are positions in a real debate, and each should be judged with reasons and evidence. questions.stem_md: A student in the imagined Greenfield school says that organising states on linguistic lines in 1956 showed that India chose to recognise the diversity of its languages rather than impose one language on everyone. Which is the best reading of this remark?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It illustrates how a democratic state can accommodate diversity by recognising language groups within the nation. questions.stem_md: The minister of imagined Marenth says: our three language communities each take part in the council, run their own evening classes and still celebrate one national day together. Which view of unity does the minister hold?
